steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on fairness scheduling for coded caching in multi-AP WiFi networks with sequential video requests. Motivate why coded caching is hard to use in practice, describe the prior CC-over-IP work we build on and its limits, and summarize what we do.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - growing data traffic, multimedia -> new communication techniques
  - on-device memory cheap; proactively store multimedia content, e.g. video-on-demand (VoD)
  - pioneering: femtocaching, F-RAN models
  - breakthrough: coded caching (CC); speedup in achievable rate scaling with cumulative cache size; multicasting carefully created codewords
  - extensions: wireless, multi-server, multi-antenna, D2D, shared-cache, multi-access, combinatorial networks
- Practical problems
  - mathematically elegant, information-theoretic optimality, but realistic application problematic
  - most wireless CC works assume PHY (e.g. multi-user MIMO precoding) jointly designed with CC
  - unlikely: new standard's PHY/MAC not designed around CC
  - CC is "application layer" (video server + clients on user devices); PHY/MAC by different standardization bodies, wider range of applications/traffic
- CC over IP
  - prior work: CC "over IP", above network layer with multicast routing
  - our starting network model: CSMA WLAN, e.g. WiFi; optimize per-user content delivery throughput with fairness criterion
  - video server -> multiple spatially distributed users via multiple APs ("helpers")
  - collision-type interference model; packets lost above interference threshold (Section II)
  - prior authors: optimized worst-case delivery time over all user requests
  - multi-round delivery method (later proved optimal for shared-cache model); graph coloring for reuse pattern; helper-user allocation
  - heuristic 'Avalanche': uses interference-free state as helpers finish; like CSMA, AP grabs channel when no other AP transmitting above threshold
- Limitations
  - heuristic, no optimality metric
  - single-request assumption unrealistic
  - VoD streaming: sequential delivery of long sequence of "video chunks"; small segments; delivered at rate (slightly) higher than playback rate
  - key metric: long-term time-averaged number of chunks delivered per unit time
- This work
  - sequential requests; computational way to find region of per-user delivery rates
  - fairness scheduling = maximize concave component-wise non-decreasing network utility over rate region
  - utility function sets fairness criterion; proportional fairness
  - two heuristics: restricting throughput region, greedy algorithm; sub-optimal, reduced complexity
  - numerical analyses

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The amount of data traffic keeps increasing, mostly because of multimedia applications, and this has made it necessary to develop new communication techniques. One interesting resource is on-device memory. It is cheap and it can be used to store a big part of multimedia content ahead of time, e.g., for video-on-demand (VoD) applications. Because of this, many researchers have looked at using onboard memory efficiently for caching. The pioneering works introduced femtocaching and F-RAN models. Then a major breakthrough was coded caching (CC), which showed that by multicasting carefully created codewords it is possible to get a speedup factor in the achievable rate that scales with the cumulative cache size in the network. Later many works extended the original CC work, for example for wireless, multi-server, multi-antenna, D2D, shared-cache, multi-access, and combinatorial networks.

These works are mathematically elegant and often give information-theoretic optimality results, but using CC in realistic scenarios is still problematic. For example, most of the works on CC in wireless networks assume that the physical layer (e.g., multi-user MIMO precoding) can be designed together with the CC scheme. This is possible in principle, but it is very unlikely that the PHY and MAC layers of a new wireless standard will be designed as a function of CC. The reason is that CC is a content distribution scheme and it is implemented at the "application layer" (i.e., it is deployed at the video server and at the video clients on the user devices), while the PHY and MAC layers are defined by completely different standardization bodies and have to serve a much wider range of applications and traffic types.

Because of this practical constraint, an earlier work considered CC "over IP", i.e., on top of an existing network layer that can do multicast routing. We start from the network model of that work, which models a carrier-sense multiple access (CSMA) wireless local area network (WLAN) such as a WiFi setup, and we study how to optimize the per-user content delivery throughput under a fairness criterion. In this network a video server sends data to multiple spatially distributed users through multiple access points (APs), which are called "helpers". The interference model is collision-type, so packets are lost if a user receives the superposition of concurrent packets from different helpers above some interference threshold (see Section II). For this model, the earlier authors optimized the worst-case delivery time over all user requests. They used a multi-round delivery method (later proved to be optimal for the shared-cache model), and first used graph coloring to build a reuse pattern for the helpers and optimized the helper-user allocation to minimize delivery time. Then they introduced a heuristic scheme called 'Avalanche' that uses the interference-free state of the users as helpers finish their multi-round delivery. The helper activation in 'Avalanche' was similar to CSMA, where an AP grabs the channel when it detects that no other AP is transmitting above its interference threshold.

- Limitations of the prior schemes
  - heuristic, no optimality guarantee
  - single request per user is not realistic for WLAN
  - VoD streaming = long sequence of small "video chunks", each delivered a bit faster than the playback rate
  - so the metric that matters is the long-term time-averaged number of chunks delivered per unit time
- This work
  - sequential requests; computational method for the per-user delivery rate region
  - fairness scheduling: maximize concave component-wise non-decreasing network utility over the region; proportional fairness
  - two lower-complexity heuristics: restricted throughput region, greedy algorithm
  - numerical analyses

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The amount of data traffic keeps increasing, mostly because of multimedia applications, and this has made it necessary to develop new communication techniques. One interesting resource is on-device memory. It is cheap and it can be used to store a big part of multimedia content ahead of time, e.g., for video-on-demand (VoD) applications. Because of this, many researchers have looked at using onboard memory efficiently for caching. The pioneering works introduced femtocaching and F-RAN models. Then a major breakthrough was coded caching (CC), which showed that by multicasting carefully created codewords it is possible to get a speedup factor in the achievable rate that scales with the cumulative cache size in the network. Later many works extended the original CC work, for example for wireless, multi-server, multi-antenna, D2D, shared-cache, multi-access, and combinatorial networks.

These works are mathematically elegant and often give information-theoretic optimality results, but using CC in realistic scenarios is still problematic. For example, most of the works on CC in wireless networks assume that the physical layer (e.g., multi-user MIMO precoding) can be designed together with the CC scheme. This is possible in principle, but it is very unlikely that the PHY and MAC layers of a new wireless standard will be designed as a function of CC. The reason is that CC is a content distribution scheme and it is implemented at the "application layer" (i.e., it is deployed at the video server and at the video clients on the user devices), while the PHY and MAC layers are defined by completely different standardization bodies and have to serve a much wider range of applications and traffic types.

Because of this practical constraint, an earlier work considered CC "over IP", i.e., on top of an existing network layer that can do multicast routing. We start from the network model of that work, which models a carrier-sense multiple access (CSMA) wireless local area network (WLAN) such as a WiFi setup, and we study how to optimize the per-user content delivery throughput under a fairness criterion. In this network a video server sends data to multiple spatially distributed users through multiple access points (APs), which are called "helpers". The interference model is collision-type, so packets are lost if a user receives the superposition of concurrent packets from different helpers above some interference threshold (see Section II). For this model, the earlier authors optimized the worst-case delivery time over all user requests. They used a multi-round delivery method (later proved to be optimal for the shared-cache model), and first used graph coloring to build a reuse pattern for the helpers and optimized the helper-user allocation to minimize delivery time. Then they introduced a heuristic scheme called 'Avalanche' that uses the interference-free state of the users as helpers finish their multi-round delivery. The helper activation in 'Avalanche' was similar to CSMA, where an AP grabs the channel when it detects that no other AP is transmitting above its interference threshold.

However, those schemes are heuristic and do not achieve any optimality metric. Also, their single-request assumption is not attractive for real-world implementation of CC in WLAN. In practice, CC applied to VoD streaming needs sequential delivery of a long sequence of "video chunks" that form the streaming session. Each chunk is a relatively small segment of a video, and the chunks have to be delivered at a rate (slightly) higher than the playback rate at which the video buffer is emptied in the user's video player application. So the most important performance metric is the delivery rate, expressed as the long-term time-averaged number of chunks delivered per unit of time.

In this work we consider sequential requests and give a computational way to find the region of per-user delivery rates. We formulate the fairness scheduling problem as maximizing a concave component-wise non-decreasing network utility function over the rate region. The fairness criterion depends on which network utility function is chosen, and here we focus on proportional fairness. We also give two heuristic methods, one based on restricting the throughput region and one greedy algorithmic approach, which reach a sub-optimal solution with lower complexity. We use numerical analyses to evaluate how the proposed solutions perform.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The increasing amount of data traffic, driven especially by multimedia applications, has necessitated the development of new communication techniques. One interesting resource is on-device memory: it is cheap and can be used to proactively store a large part of multimedia content, e.g., for video-on-demand (VoD) applications. As a result, many researchers have considered the efficient use of onboard memory in the context of caching. Pioneering works in this regard introduced femtocaching [1] and F-RAN models [2]. A major breakthrough came with the introduction of coded caching (CC) [3], which showed that a speedup factor in the achievable rate, scaling with the cumulative cache size in the network, is possible by multicasting carefully created codewords. Later, many works extended the original CC work of [3], e.g., to wireless [4], multi-server [5], multi-antenna [6], D2D [7], shared-cache [8], multi-access [9], and combinatorial [10] networks.

While these works are mathematically elegant and often yield information-theoretic optimality results [11], applying CC in realistic scenarios remains problematic. For example, most works treating CC on wireless networks assume that the physical layer (e.g., multi-user MIMO precoding) can be jointly designed with the CC scheme [12,13]. While this is possible in principle, it is highly unlikely that the PHY and MAC layers of a new wireless standard would be designed as a function of CC. This is because CC, as a content distribution scheme, is implemented at the "application layer" (i.e., deployed at the video server and at the video clients running on the user devices), while the PHY and MAC layers are defined by completely different standardization bodies and must serve a much wider range of applications and traffic types.

Recognizing this practical constraint, the work [14] considered CC "over IP", i.e., above an existing network layer capable of multicast routing. The present work starts from the network model of [14], which models a carrier-sense multiple access (CSMA) wireless local area network (WLAN), such as a WiFi setup, and studies the optimization of per-user content delivery throughput subject to a fairness criterion. In the considered network, a video server transmits data to multiple spatially distributed users through multiple access points (APs), referred to as "helpers". A collision-type interference model is used, so that packets are lost if a user receives the superposition of concurrent packets from different helpers above a certain interference threshold (see Section II). For this network model, the authors of [14] optimized the worst-case delivery time over all user requests. Using the multi-round delivery method in [15] (later proved by [8] to be optimal for the shared-cache model), they first used graph coloring to construct a reuse pattern for the helpers and optimized the helper-user allocation to minimize the delivery time. Next, they introduced a heuristic scheme dubbed 'Avalanche' to leverage the interference-free state of the users as helpers finished their multi-round delivery. Helper activation in 'Avalanche' was reminiscent of CSMA, where an AP grabs the channel when it detects that no other AP is transmitting above its interference threshold.

The schemes in [14] are heuristic and do not achieve any optimality metric. Moreover, the single-request assumption of [14] is not appealing for a real-world implementation of CC in WLAN. In practice, CC applied to VoD streaming requires the sequential delivery of a long sequence of "video chunks" forming the streaming session. Each chunk contains a relatively small segment of a video, and the chunks must be delivered at a rate (slightly) higher than the playback rate at which the video buffer is emptied at the user's video player application. Hence, the most important performance metric is the delivery rate, expressed as the long-term time-averaged number of chunks delivered per unit of time.

In this work, we consider sequential requests and present a computational way to determine the region of per-user delivery rates. The fairness scheduling problem is formulated as the maximization of a concave component-wise non-decreasing network utility function over the rate region. The choice of the network utility function determines the fairness criterion; here we focus on proportional fairness [16]. We also provide two heuristic methods, based on restricting the throughput region and on a greedy algorithmic approach, that achieve a sub-optimal solution with reduced complexity. Numerical analyses are used to evaluate the performance of the proposed solutions.
